\section{Summary}\label{sec:summary}
An LFU cache controller for embedding lookups was implemented in two versions. v2 (tag \texttt{rtl-v2-final}) breaks
ties between lines of equal count by the lowest slot index; v3 (tag \texttt{rtl-v3-final}) adds the Rotate-victim
tie-break, one pointer register and one extra key bit. Both were taken through an open-source flow (Yosys, OpenSTA,
NanGate45; pre-layout) as a baseline, and through a commercial flow with an STMicroelectronics 28nm FD-SOI
standard-cell library (accessed through CMP): Cadence Genus synthesis, Xcelium gate-level simulation, Genus power
analysis from simulated activity, Innovus place and route, and re-timing of the routed designs at three corners.
Table~\ref{tab:summary} gives the headline results. Each design point was run once, so differences between v2 and v3
smaller than the same-logic synthesis variation of Section~\ref{sec:p12} are not evidence of a design effect; no
variation between repeated layouts was measured (Section~\ref{sec:p15}).

Three results stand out. First, both versions meet the same clock period in synthesis and after routing at the
typical corner, and the place-and-route bracket is looser than the synthesis bracket because routing adds wire delay
and a real clock tree. Second, v3 needs \R{p15.dE.row1M.abs} to \R{p15.dE.row0.abs}\% less energy per request
after routing, because its higher hit rate shortens the run, while its power is slightly higher. Third, the layouts
were optimised at the typical corner only: at the slow corner setup fails, and I/O hold checks fail for a reason
traced in Section~\ref{sec:p16}. Registers and the clock tree take nearly all of the power, which points to clock
gating or SRAM storage as the next design step.

\section{Design under test}\label{sec:design}
\subsection{Controller}
The controller (Fig.~\ref{fig:rtl}, Table~\ref{tab:params}) keeps tags, data words, frequency counters and valid bits
in flip-flops; there is no SRAM. Each line holds a \R{rtl.vecw}-bit data word, not a whole embedding vector. The FSM
has four states. In IDLE a request is accepted and its address registered, together with one copy of the address per
group of lines (the per-group address flip-flops), which split the fan-out of the address to the tag comparators. In
LOOKUP each group compares its lines' tags with its address copy, an OR of the match bits gives the hit flag, and a
balanced priority tree gives the index of the matching line. On a hit the counter of that line is incremented
(saturating at \R{rtl.sat}) and the data returned, and the FSM goes back to IDLE.

On a miss the victim is chosen in two stages. Stage~A, a minimum tree inside each group, is registered at the end of
LOOKUP; Stage~B, a minimum tree across the group minima, runs in EVICT. The key of a line is
$\mathit{eff}$: zero for an invalid line and the count plus one for a valid line, so invalid lines fill first. In FILL
the controller waits for the returned data, writes tag, data and valid bit into the victim line and sets its count.
The parameter \texttt{COUNTER\_MODE} selects the count of a new line: in mode 0 it starts at one (an LFU with counters
reset on eviction); in mode 1, the original behaviour, it continues from the count left in the slot. Mode 0 is the
design point of this report; mode 1 serves as a same-logic reference (Section~\ref{sec:p12}).

\subsection{v2 and v3}
Both minimum trees keep their left operand unless the right one is strictly smaller, so in v2 the victim among the
lines of smallest count is the one with the lowest slot index. Because new lines start at count one, this tie-break
evicts the most recently installed line almost every time, which is why v2 loses to LRU in trace simulation (see the
paper). v3 (phase P10) adds a pointer register \texttt{ptr} that loads victim${}+1$ (modulo the depth) when a
fill completes, and extends both tree keys by one wrap bit, set for slots below \texttt{ptr}. The victim is then the
first minimum-count slot at or after \texttt{ptr}, wrapping around; the key grows to \R{p10.kw} bits. Tree depth,
counters and FSM are unchanged, and mode 1 keeps the v2 rule (its wrap bit is constant).

The added state is the pointer only. In the Genus netlists of mode 0 the flip-flop count grows by exactly the
pointer width at every depth (Table~\ref{tab:ff}). These netlists do not contain the per-group address flip-flops,
because Genus merged them (Section~\ref{sec:mergeoff}).

\section{Verification before implementation}\label{sec:verif}
The RTL was verified before any implementation run, and every netlist simulated later was compared with its RTL cycle
by cycle (Table~\ref{tab:verif}). The self-checking testbench of v2 has \R{rtl.tests} tests; v3 adds a tie-order test
that checks the victim order and the pointer wrap-around, and catches all \R{p10.mut} mutants of the new rule.
Mutation testing checks that the tests can fail: each mutant is a deliberately broken copy of the RTL, and every
mutant that changes behaviour must be killed. Some mutants, such as a reversed tie order in a tree, pass the unit
tests and are caught only by lockstep comparison of the victim slot against a reference. The RTL-exact model (P9) is a
software model of the controller's victim selection; in lockstep with it, the v3 RTL agrees request by request on
slices of the Criteo access stream (P10).

\section{Open-source baseline flow}\label{sec:open}
\emph{All results in this section are pre-layout and use the NanGate45 open library, a different library from the
28nm FD-SOI library of the following sections; they are a baseline for the design changes, not a prediction of the
28nm results.}

\subsection{Flow}
Phases P5 to P8 used Yosys \R{tool.yosys} with ABC~\cite{wolf_yosys,brayton2010abc} to map the RTL to the NanGate45
library~\cite{nangate45} at its typical corner, OpenSTA \R{tool.opensta}~\cite{opensta} for setup and hold analysis
with the library's wire-load model (\texttt{5K\_hvratio\_1\_1}) and an ideal clock, and Icarus Verilog~\cite{icarus}
for simulation. Area is the sum of cell areas in \umsq, not a placed area. Each configuration (three depths, mode 0
and mode 1) was synthesised for a \R{clk.1000}\,MHz and a \R{clk.500}\,MHz target; Fmax is the reciprocal of the
clock period minus the worst setup slack.

\subsection{Timing restructuring and Fmax}
The baseline (P5) met neither target. Three RTL changes replaced serial loops by balanced trees
(Table~\ref{tab:p5iter}, Fig.~\ref{fig:fmax}): a Stage-B tree with the per-group address flip-flops (P5b), a Stage-A
tree (P5c) and a hit-index priority tree (P5d, which became \texttt{rtl-v2-final}). For P5c a rule was fixed before
synthesis: keep the address flip-flops only if, at depth \R{sz.256}, Fmax with them is at least \R{p5c.rule} times
Fmax without them; they gave \R{p5c.copy.m0}\% (mode 0) and \R{p5c.copy.m1}\% (mode 1) and were kept, a margin
that P5d later found to lie inside the flow noise floor. Every change was checked by the
unchanged unit tests and by lockstep against the earlier versions.

P5e then changed the flow, not the RTL. The delay target passed to ABC could not bind when ABC's own estimate was
above both targets, and ABC's timer ran without the wire-load model and without the flip-flop clock-to-output and
setup times. The timing-driven flow runs three delay-oriented ABC passes, buffering and sizing with the wire-load
model, and an ABC target of the period minus \R{p5e.budget}\,ps. On the same RTL it raises Fmax beyond the noise band
at every depth (Table~\ref{tab:p5iter}, Fig.~\ref{fig:fmax}); Table~\ref{tab:p5e} gives the final netlists.

\subsection{Flow noise floor}
P5d synthesised eight designs with identical logic: the final RTL, a flat-vector form of it, and three one-line
rewrites of each. Over both modes the flow alone moves their Fmax by up to \R{p5d.noise.64.1}\% on the old flow, and by
\R{p5e.noise.64.1} to \R{p5e.noise.16.0}\% on the timing-driven flow (P5d, P5e; Table~\ref{tab:p5iter} shows mode 0). Differences between two
designs smaller than this spread are not evidence of a design effect. The \R{clk.500}\,MHz netlists meet timing at
depths \R{sz.16} and \R{sz.64}; at depth \R{sz.256} they miss by amounts far inside the noise, so whether depth
\R{sz.256} meets \R{clk.500}\,MHz is not shown either way. The same reasoning applies to v3: synthesised with the
unchanged P5e flow (P11), every Fmax change of v3 in mode 0 lies within the \R{p11.nnoise}\% change seen between the
two versions in mode 1, whose logic is the same, so no Fmax cost or gain of Rotate-victim is claimed.

\subsection{Gate-level simulation and equivalence}
Phase P5f simulated all \R{p5f.netlists} netlists with zero delay, using cell models generated by Yosys from the
library and checked against the library's cell functions (\R{p5f.pass} of \R{p5f.cells} passed; the one failure is
a flip-flop with both set and reset that no netlist uses). In lockstep with the RTL over \R{p5f.cycles} random cycles,
comparing hit flag, response valid, response data, fill request and fill address every cycle, no netlist shows a
mismatching cycle or an unknown output. Yosys proves the four depth-\R{sz.16} netlists equivalent to the RTL
(\R{p5f.eq} equivalence cells); the proof treats the asynchronous reset as synchronous.

\subsection{Power analysis and the clock-pin bias}
Phase P8 ran OpenSTA power analysis on the \R{clk.500}\,MHz netlists with activity from zero-delay gate-level
simulation (Table~\ref{tab:p8}). The clock-pin energy of the flip-flops dominates: each flip-flop spends nearly the
same recalculated energy on its clock pin in every cycle (\R{p8.ckff}\,fJ per cycle at depth \R{sz.256}). OpenSTA
weights the clock-pin energy by state probabilities that it treats as independent; in a test on one netlist, a
per-event recomputation from the activity file differed from OpenSTA by \R{p8.bias}\%, so the clock-pin term in
Table~\ref{tab:p8} is the recalculated one. The figures are labelled NanGate45, typical corner, pre-layout, no clock
tree, flip-flop storage, random fill data, activity over \R{p8.cycles} cycles of the row0 slice.

\section{28nm FD-SOI synthesis}\label{sec:p12}
\subsection{Setup}
All 28nm work ran on a laboratory server with Cadence tools. The library files stay on that server and are never
opened, printed or copied by the project (only the tools read them); only aggregate tables generated from the tool reports of the project's own runs are published. Genus
(phase P12) used the typical-corner timing libraries, a constraint file with one clock, no clock uncertainty, and
input and output delays of \R{p12.io} times the period on the ideal clock. No physical data were read: the wire
load is the library default, which is zero, so the netlists are timed without wire capacitance. Genus states no
area unit, so synthesis areas are given in library units. Power at this stage is vectorless (default switching
activity) and is not used in this report.

v2 and v3, both modes and all three depths were synthesised at six clock periods from \R{p12.per.max} ns down to
\R{p12.per.min} ns. The worst setup slack (WNS) of each run decides whether the period is met.

\subsection{Timing brackets}
The Fmax of a failing run, the reciprocal of the period minus WNS, depends on the target period, because the synthesised
netlist itself changes with the target. For v2 at depth \R{sz.64} in mode 0 it is \R{sr.fx.v2.64.065}\,MHz
from the \R{sr.per.065} ns run (WNS \R{sr.wns.v2.64.065} ps) but \R{sr.fx.v2.64.05}\,MHz from the \R{p12.per.min} ns
run (WNS \R{sr.wns.v2.64.05} ps). The reliable figure is therefore the bracket: the tightest period met and the
loosest period failed (Table~\ref{tab:p12}). At depths \R{sz.16} and \R{sz.256} the brackets are the same for all
four version and mode pairs; at depth \R{sz.64} only v3 in mode 1 differs, by one step. At depth \R{sz.256} both
versions meet \R{p12.br.256.met} ns and fail \R{p12.br.256.fail} ns.

\subsection{Area and the same-logic noise reference}
At the relaxed \R{p12.relax} ns period every run meets timing, at depth \R{sz.256} with almost no slack left, so
area still reflects some timing effort there (Table~\ref{tab:p12area}). Mode 1 is the same logic in v2 and v3 (proven at depths
\R{sz.16} and \R{sz.64}), so its v3$-$v2 difference is the observed noise of the flow. In mode 0 the area of v3
differs from v2 by at most \R{p12.a.16.m0.abs}\%, while the same-logic differences in mode 1 reach
\R{p12.a.256.m1.abs}\%; Rotate-victim therefore has no area cost that this flow can resolve. At tight periods the
same-logic area difference reaches \R{p12.noise}\%, so areas at tight periods are not compared.

\subsection{The per-group address flip-flops (merge-off)}\label{sec:mergeoff}
Genus recognised the per-group address copies as equivalent registers and merged them into one, so the normal
netlists lack the fan-out split the RTL was written for. A second set of runs at depth \R{sz.256}, mode 0, disabled
this merging for those registers only (\emph{merge-off}). All \R{p12.copies} address flip-flops are then kept: the
flip-flop count rises from \R{sr.mo.v2.065.n.ff} to \R{sr.mo.v2.065.mo.ff} for v2 and from \R{sr.mo.v3.065.n.ff} to
\R{sr.mo.v3.065.mo.ff} for v3. At \R{p12.br.256.fail} ns, where both flows fail, merge-off raises Fmax from
\R{p12.f.v2} to \R{p12.fmo.v2}\,MHz for v2 (\R{p12.mo.v2}\%) and from \R{p12.f.v3} to \R{p12.fmo.v3}\,MHz for v3
(\R{p12.mo.v3}\%), one run each. The area change in those failing runs is \R{p12.fmo.a.v2}\% for v2 and
\R{p12.mo.a.v3}\% for v3, the latter above every same-logic difference; at \R{p13.period} ns, where both flows
meet timing, it is \R{sr.p12.mo.a08.v2}\% for v2 and \R{sr.p12.mo.a08.v3}\% for v3. The merge-off netlists
synthesised at \R{p13.period} ns are the ones taken to gate-level simulation and place and route.

% ===================================================================================================================
\section{Gate-level simulation and power before layout}\label{sec:p13}
\subsection{Lockstep simulation}
The merge-off depth-\R{sz.256} netlists of v2 and v3 (mode 0, \R{p13.period} ns) were simulated with Xcelium
(phase P13) on the two Criteo slices of \R{p13.req} requests each, in lockstep with their RTL: the testbench drives
both with the same requests and compares the outputs every cycle. Each slice was run twice, with zero delay and with
the SDF written by Genus; in the SDF runs the inputs change \R{sr.p13.indelay} ps after the clock edge, as in the
constraints. All runs show no mismatching cycle and no unknown value, and the netlist hit logs equal those of the RTL
line for line.

\subsection{SDF annotation coverage}
The SDF runs annotate the path delays (v3: \R{sr.p13.pd.v3} of \R{sr.p13.pdn.v3}; v2: \R{sr.p13.pd.v2} of
\R{sr.p13.pdn.v2}) but none of the timing checks (v3: \R{sr.p13.tc.v3} of \R{sr.p13.tcn.v3}). The timing checks of
the cell simulation models are conditional, and the SDF written by Genus has no conditional entries, so the
simulator finds no matching check to annotate. \R{p13.variants} variants of the SDF writer options were tried, all
with the same result. A gate-level run without timing checks cannot detect setup or hold violations, so these runs
confirm the function of the netlists with real path delays, not their timing; timing rests on static analysis.

\subsection{Power from simulated activity}
Genus computed power from the toggle counts (TCF) of each SDF run. Flip-flop outputs and ports are fully annotated;
of the combinational driver nets only \R{p13.cov.lo} to \R{p13.cov.hi}\% are, and Genus propagates activity to the
rest. Combinational logic takes \R{p13.logic.lo} to \R{p13.logic.hi}\% of the power, so its share is taken as the
bound on the error from the missing activity. Energy per request is power times cycles times period, divided by the
number of requests (Table~\ref{tab:p13}). Registers take \R{p13.reg.lo} to \R{p13.reg.hi}\% of the power: storing
every line in flip-flops dominates.

v3 needs \R{p13.dE.row1M.abs} to \R{p13.dE.row0.abs}\% less energy per request than v2. Its power is slightly higher,
but its higher hit rate means fewer requests wait for a fill, and the same requests take \R{p13.dC.row0.abs}\% and
\R{p13.dC.row1M.abs}\% fewer cycles. The cycle count depends on the testbench's fill model, which answers a miss after
\R{p13.fill.lo} to \R{p13.fill.hi} random cycles rather than modelling a memory system.

\section{Place and route}\label{sec:p15}
\subsection{Flow}
Innovus (phase P15) placed and routed the merge-off depth-\R{sz.256} netlists of both versions and the depth-\R{sz.16}
netlist of v3, all synthesised at \R{p13.period} ns, at the typical corner (\R{p15.tt.v}\,V, \R{p15.tt.t}\,\textdegree C,
nominal RC extraction). The final flow has these steps:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Multi-row cells excluded.} All library cells taller than one row (\R{p15.dontuse} of them) are not to
be used, and multi-row instances in the netlist are resized to single-row cells before the floorplan
(Section~\ref{sec:issues}).
\item \textbf{Floorplan.} A square core sized from a fixed target utilisation, with a margin to the die edge; inputs on
one side of the block and outputs on the opposite side.
\item \textbf{Row ends and corners.} End caps on the left and right ends of every row and in the top and bottom rows,
and end caps also at the four core corners.
\item \textbf{Well taps.} Well-tap cells in a checkerboard pattern; they connect the transistor bodies to the
body-bias nets.
\item \textbf{Power grid.} A four-net grid of rings, row rails, stripes and vias for the supply, the ground and the
two body-bias nets of FD-SOI. The well-tap body pins are routed to the body-bias nets with the signal nets; the
other cells join them by abutment along each row.
\item \textbf{Placement and clock tree.} Placement with optimisation, then clock-tree synthesis with the clock
buffers and inverters of the library only, followed by hold optimisation. A setup target slack of \R{p15.tslack} ns
applies to all optimisation steps of the depth-\R{sz.256} runs (the depth-\R{sz.16} run predates it).
\item \textbf{Routing and post-route optimisation.} Routing, setup and hold optimisation, filler insertion and
DRC repair, a DRC check with a second repair pass, and one more post-route setup optimisation (fillers removed and
re-inserted). At the two tightest periods, two further post-route hold passes, the second with a hold target slack of
\R{sr.htarget} ns.
\item \textbf{Checks.} Setup and hold timing, DRC, connectivity of all nets and of the four power nets, the same
connectivity check through metal only (without the well connection), and the well-tap distance check.
\end{enumerate}
Each full depth-\R{sz.256} place-and-route run took \R{p15.rt.min} to \R{p15.rt.max} (wall time,
hours:minutes:seconds) on \R{sr.cpus} CPUs, with several runs sharing the server; a hold pass took a few minutes.

\subsection{Post-route gate-level simulation and power}
Simulation and power after routing used the \R{p15.gls.period} ns layouts, which meet setup and hold at the typical

extracted parasitics (SPEF). Lockstep simulation as in Section~\ref{sec:p13}, with SDF inputs \R{sr.p15.indelay} ps after
the clock edge, showed no mismatching cycle with zero delay and with SDF. The SDF path delays are \R{p15.sdf.path}\%
annotated and the timing checks \R{p15.sdf.check}\%, as before layout; the cause was not traced for the Innovus
SDF, which, unlike the Genus SDF, does contain conditional entries. Genus computed power from
the routed netlist, the parasitics (v2: \R{sr.p15.spef.v2} nets, \R{sr.p15.spef0.v2} not annotated) and the toggle
counts of the SDF run (Table~\ref{tab:p15pow}).

v3 needs \R{p15.dE.row1M.abs} to \R{p15.dE.row0.abs}\% less energy per request than v2, again because it needs fewer

but \R{p15.logic.lo} to \R{p15.logic.hi}\% of the power, and the clock tree alone \R{p15.clk.lo} to
\R{p15.clk.hi}\%. Storing every line in flip-flops that are clocked every cycle dominates the power, which makes
clock gating or SRAM storage the next design step.

\section{Corners}\label{sec:p16}
\subsection{Re-timing without re-optimisation}
The layouts were placed, clock-tree synthesised, routed and optimised at the typical corner only. Phase P16 restored
the routed designs, added a slow corner (\R{p16.ss.v}\,V, \R{p16.ss.t}\,\textdegree C, maximum-RC extraction) and a
fast corner (\R{p16.ff.v}\,V, \R{p16.ff.t}\,\textdegree C, minimum-C extraction), re-extracted the parasitics per
corner, and re-timed each design without changing it (Table~\ref{tab:p16}). Typical-corner re-timing reproduces the
place-and-route reports exactly. Setup fails at the slow corner for every design and is met at the fast corner with
at least \R{sr.ff.s.lo} ns of slack. None of the designs meets setup and hold at all three corners; this is expected
for layouts optimised at one corner and is not a flow error.

The derived slow-corner period, the place-and-route period minus the slow-corner setup WNS of the same layout, is
\R{p16.dp.v2.10} ns for v2 and \R{p16.dp.v3.10} ns for v3 at \R{p15.met} ns. It is not a measurement: it ignores
hold and assumes the layout would not change at the new period. Here v3 is ahead, the opposite sign to the
typical-corner difference at \R{p15.fail} ns, which suggests that both differences lie within the variation of the
flow.

\subsection{Why the I/O hold checks fail}
At the slow corner hold fails for the depth-\R{sz.256} layouts in the I/O path group only; register-to-register hold
is met. Path reports traced on the v3 \R{p15.met} ns layout explain this. The constraints give the inputs a delay of
\R{p16.io.indelay} ns relative to the ideal edge of the external clock, but the capturing register's clock arrives at
\R{p16.io.clk} ns through the propagated clock tree, so the hold slack is \R{p16.io.slack} ns. Of the failing paths
all but \R{d.in2reg.other} start at an input, and no register-to-output path fails: a later launch clock only adds
margin there.

At the typical corner the same path passes with \R{p16.io.ttslack} ns, because the saved database holds, for the
typical view only, a clock source latency of \R{p16.io.lat} ns that the tool wrote during the flow (the flow scripts
set none). It cancels the \R{p16.io.tree} ns clock-tree delay for I/O paths. The added slow and fast views have no
such latency. The failures therefore come from I/O delays referenced to an ideal external clock against a propagated
internal clock, compensated only in the view the design was built in. At the fast corner hold fails mostly in the
I/O group as well, and in the \R{p15.met} ns layouts also on a few register-to-register paths (\R{p16.ff.hrr.v2} for
v2, \R{p16.ff.hrr.v3} for v3).

\subsection{What sign-off would require}
Sign-off of these blocks would need, first, block-level I/O constraints with a clock latency for every corner (or
I/O timing budgets derived from the surrounding design), and second, multi-corner optimisation, so that setup at the
slow corner and hold at the fast corner are fixed in the same layout. A separate sign-off timing tool and physical
verification (DRC and LVS against the foundry rule deck) would replace the Innovus checks used here.

\textbf{Frequency.} Synthesis meets \R{p12.br.256.met} ns, routing \R{p15.met} ns. Synthesis times the netlist with
zero wire load and an ideal clock. After routing, extracted wire capacitance and resistance add delay to every net,
and the propagated clock tree adds skew between launch and capture registers; hold fixing can add delay on short
paths. The step from \R{p12.br.256.met} to \R{p15.met} ns is the combined cost of these effects for this design.

\textbf{Area.} Genus states no area unit, while Innovus reports \umsq, so the two columns are not compared
numerically. The core is sized from the target utilisation; the space not used by logic cells holds end caps, well
taps and fillers.

\textbf{Power.} The two power figures belong to different clock periods and different models, so their ratio is not
a layout cost. Before layout there is no clock tree and no wire capacitance, and the switching power is small. After
routing the switching power includes the clock tree and the routed nets, and is many times larger even at the longer
period; the clock tree alone takes \R{p15.clk.v2.row0}\% of the power of v2. The relative energy saving of v3 is
similar at both stages (\R{p13.dE.row0.abs}\% before and \R{p15.dE.row0.abs}\% after layout on slice row0), because
it comes from the cycle count, which layout does not change.

\section{Limitations and next steps}\label{sec:limits}
\subsection{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{One corner.} Placement, clock tree, routing and optimisation used the typical corner only; slow-corner
setup fails and, at depth \R{sz.256}, slow- and fast-corner hold fail (Section~\ref{sec:p16}).
\item \textbf{One run per point.} Every synthesis period and every layout was run once. The only noise references
are the same-logic synthesis pairs in mode 1; there is no same-logic pair of layouts, so v2 against v3 differences in
post-route timing and area cannot be separated from flow variation.
\item \textbf{Flow dependence.} Fmax from a failing synthesis run depends on the target period, and the open-flow
noise floor is large; brackets are the reliable figure.
\item \textbf{Timing checks not annotated.} No gate-level simulation annotated the cell timing checks, so zero
violations in simulation is not a timing check; timing rests on static analysis.
\item \textbf{Activity coverage.} Combinational driver nets are only partly annotated in power analysis
(\R{p15.cov.v2}\% and \R{p15.cov.v3}\% after routing); the combinational share bounds the error.
\item \textbf{Testbench fill model.} Cycles, and hence energy per request, depend on the testbench's random fill
latency, not on a memory system, and on two slices of one dataset.
\item \textbf{Checks.} Innovus checks only; no separate sign-off timing, DRC or LVS.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Next steps}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Multi-corner sign-off:} per-corner I/O constraints with clock latency, multi-corner optimisation, and
repeated layouts of the same netlist to measure place-and-route variation.
\item \textbf{Clock gating or SRAM storage:} registers and the clock tree take nearly all of the power; gating the
clock of idle lines, or holding the data array in an SRAM macro, addresses the largest term.
\item \textbf{Set-associative controller:} the fully associative victim search sets the pre-layout critical path
on NanGate45 (P5d); a set-associative organisation with Rotate-victim per set would shorten that search.
\item \textbf{Memory model:} replace the testbench fill model by a DRAM model, so that energy per request reflects
real miss latency.
\end{itemize}

P16 & \path{<design>} with the corner name & restored P15 layouts re-timed at the slow and fast corners &
\path{results/P16/} \\

\end{tabularx}
